sections.title: Behavioral Change for Social Impact: A Human-Centered Approach
sections.description: How do we gather and utilize the most valuable insights on, for example, how extreme poverty persists and can be addressed in the Kazmain locality of Lucknow, India? Would the most meaningful insights come from (i) a noted economics professor at Wharton, (ii) a senior technical advisor on poverty reduction at the World Bank’s India country office, (iii) an individual living in extreme poverty within Kazmain, or (iv) elsewhere? This course examines behavioral change interventions across a broad scope of topics in international development, using a human-centered, decolonized, and ethics-based approach. Our analysis of the successes, failures, and effectiveness of interventions will be rooted in the thinking that human-centered design, implementation, and evaluation of interventions is the most impactful and sustainable way of promoting positive behavioral change. Over the semester, we will study an array of behavioral change interventions linked to poverty, inequality, climate change, water and sanitation, education, health, food security, livelihoods, conflict resolution, displacement, and corruption. Case studies will (tentatively) cover interventions in Afghanistan, China, Ecuador, Greece, Haiti, India, Palestine, Lebanon, South Africa, South Sudan, the United States, and Yemen. The class will be highly participatory–using a mixture of the case method and seminar-style discussion–and will encourage intellectual curiosity, discovery, empathy, and dissent. Note: While priority for registration will be given to Behavioral and Decision Sciences students, all Penn students are welcome to register for this course.
